article.title: Vote Yes on Proposition 4: Democracy Shouldn’t Depend on Wealth
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. A person should not need wealthy friends to run for public office. And a voter’s influence should not depend on the size of a campaign contribution. Those principles sound basic. Yet when raising money becomes the first test of political viability, people with deep pockets gain an advantage before voters ever hear the candidates debate. Community knowledge, public service, and good ideas can take a back seat to access to donors. California’s Proposition 4, the California Fair Elections Act, offers a practical step toward changing that imbalance. On November 3, vote yes. Give communities the power to act Proposition 4 would remove California’s prohibition on public campaign financing for most state and local offices. It would allow governments to establish programs that give qualifying candidates public support for their campaigns. It would not automatically create or fund those programs. That would require subsequent decisions. California Secretary of State That distinction matters. Voters are deciding whether communities should have this tool available at all. Some California cities already do. Los Angeles, San Francisco, Long Beach, Oakland, and Berkeley operate public campaign financing programs under an exception for charter cities. Proposition 4 would open the door more broadly. Why should a community willing to build a fairer campaign system be barred from trying? Make ordinary supporters matter more Consider a nurse, teacher, tenant organizer, or small-business owner with strong community support but few connections to major donors. Running a credible campaign requires reaching voters, and reaching voters costs money. A well-designed public financing program can help bridge that gap. One option is to match small donations with public funds, increasing the value of contributions from ordinary supporters. The Yes on 4 campaign identifies small-donor matching as one model communities could adopt. Proposition 4 itself does not require that particular approach. The democratic promise is straightforward: candidates could have a stronger reason to build broad community support and a better opportunity to compete without relying so heavily on wealthy benefactors. No financing system guarantees good leadership. But fundraising connections should not determine who gets a serious chance to offer it. For progressives, this reaches beyond campaign procedure. The ability to compete for office shapes who can influence housing, wages, healthcare, environmental protection, and public investment. If we want government to respond to people whose needs are routinely overlooked, we should care about the barriers between those people and elected office. Safeguards—and work still to do Proposition 4 includes restrictions. Funds earmarked for education, transportation, or public safety could not finance campaigns. Candidates receiving public funds would have to meet eligibility requirements and accept spending limits. The money could not cover legal defense costs, fines, or repayment of candidates’ personal campaign loans. Opponents object to spending taxpayer money on campaigns and argue that too many details are left to future policymakers. Those concerns deserve a direct answer: public financing must have clear budgets, transparent reporting, enforceable rules, and meaningful oversight. The Legislative Analyst says future programs could carry significant costs, depending on their design. The measure itself would also produce a few hundred thousand dollars in annual state costs for guidance. Supporting Proposition 4 means accepting responsibility for scrutinizing what comes next. It also means being honest about its limits. The measure does not eliminate private campaign money or guarantee that wealthy interests will lose influence. It permits communities to build an alternative to candidates’ dependence on that money. The League of Women Voters of California, California Nurses Association, California Common Cause, and Consumer Watchdog are among the organizations backing that opportunity. Open the door Frustration with big money in politics is justified. Resignation gives that money a permanent advantage. Proposition 4 offers a concrete action: let California communities create public financing systems that can help qualified candidates compete and give ordinary supporters greater weight. If you have not voted, vote yes on Proposition 4 . If you have, tell friends why it matters. We should judge candidates by their ideas, integrity, and service to their communities. California should give more of them a fair chance to be heard.
